title: Coffee, tea, yerba mate and matcha: caffeine comparison

seo.title: Coffee, tea, mate and matcha: caffeine comparison
seo.meta_description: Coffee: 80–100 mg/8 oz; tea: 30–50 mg/8 oz; 2 g matcha: roughly 38–89 mg; mate can be around 80 mg/150 ml. Preparation matters.
seo.search_intent: Compare caffeine in coffee, tea, yerba mate and matcha

excerpt: There is no universal cup. As a broad guide, the FDA lists brewed coffee at about 80–100 mg caffeine per 8 fl oz and green or black tea at 30–50 mg. Two grams of matcha could provide roughly 38–89 mg based on published dry-powder analyses; a yerba-mate review reports about 80 mg in a 150 ml cup, with repeated traditional pours potentially raising the session total much higher.
content_html:
Asking which drink has the most caffeine sounds easy until serving size enters the picture. A 1-ounce espresso, 12-ounce drip coffee, repeatedly refilled mate and 1- versus 3-gram matcha are not equivalent servings.

The numbers below are therefore useful reference servings, not fixed laboratory constants.

DrinkReference servingApprox. caffeine
Brewed coffee8 fl oz80–100 mg
Green or black tea8 fl oz30–50 mg
Matcha2 g powder~38–89 mg
Yerba mate150 ml~80 mg in one review

Coffee is usually high, but serving size can reverse rankings

An 8-ounce coffee is commonly 80–100 mg according to FDA guidance. A larger shop coffee can exceed that, while a small espresso may contain less total caffeine despite being more concentrated per ounce.

Tea depends heavily on extraction

Green and black tea commonly fall around 30–50 mg per 8 ounces, but more leaf, hotter water and longer steeping can raise extraction.

Matcha depends on grams of powder

At a published range of 18.9–44.4 mg/g, 1 g matcha is about 19–44 mg, 2 g about 38–89 mg, and 3 g about 57–133 mg.

Mate is a session, not always one cup

A review reports about 80 mg caffeine in roughly 150 ml yerba mate, but traditional consumption repeatedly adds water to the same leaves. Total intake across a session can exceed 260 mg in the review's cited examples.

Count milligrams across the day

The FDA cites 400 mg/day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects for most healthy adults, while individual sensitivity, pregnancy, medications and health circumstances can require different limits.

The beverage name matters, but dose and preparation matter just as much.

faq.question: Which has more caffeine, coffee or tea?
faq.answer: Broadly, brewed coffee at 80–100 mg per 8 oz versus green or black tea at 30–50 mg per 8 oz.

faq.question: How much caffeine is in 2 g matcha?
faq.answer: Roughly 38–89 mg using the published 18.9–44.4 mg/g range.

faq.question: Is yerba mate as caffeinated as coffee?
faq.answer: It can be in the same general range. One review reports about 80 mg per 150 ml, and repeated pours can raise total intake substantially.

faq.question: Is 400 mg a limit for everyone?
faq.answer: No. It is an FDA reference for most healthy adults, not a personalized target for every person.
